module_title: PIL, Basic Structure Doctrine, and the S.R. Bommai Safeguards
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, Judiciary, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the evolution of Judicial Activism, the constitutional safeguards against the misuse of President's Rule, and the ultimate limitation on Parliament's amending power.

core_concepts.title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) & Locus Standi
core_concepts.description:
Traditionally, only the aggrieved party could approach the court (rule of 'Locus Standi'). 
- Judicial Activism: In the 1980s, Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer relaxed this rule. Through PIL (Epistolary Jurisdiction), any public-spirited citizen or NGO can approach the court on behalf of the poor, ignorant, or oppressed who cannot afford legal representation. Even a postcard can be treated as a writ petition.

core_concepts.title: Basic Structure Doctrine (Limits of Article 368)
core_concepts.description:
Can Parliament use Article 368 to rewrite the entire Constitution? 
- The Supreme Court in the historic *Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)* ruled: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, BUT it cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' or foundational framework of the Constitution (e.g., secularism, federalism, judicial review, parliamentary democracy). Any amendment violating the basic structure will be struck down.

core_concepts.title: President's Rule: Article 356 vs. Article 365
core_concepts.description:
Advanced exams test this subtle difference:
- Article 356: Imposed when the President is satisfied (via Governor's report or otherwise) that the state government cannot be carried on in accordance with constitutional provisions.
- Article 365: Imposed when a state fails to comply with or give effect to any legally valid directions given by the Union. In this case, it is 'deemed' that constitutional machinery has failed, triggering Article 356.

core_concepts.title: S.R. Bommai Case (1994): Anti-Misuse Safeguards
core_concepts.description:
Historically, the Center heavily misused Article 356 to dismiss rival state governments. The S.R. Bommai judgment established strict guidelines:
- The President's rule is subject to **Judicial Review**. The court can strike it down if found mala fide.
- The State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved until Parliament approves the proclamation.
- The only place to test a Chief Minister's majority is on the floor of the Legislative Assembly (Floor Test), not the Governor's subjective opinion.

important_entities.name: Judicial Review (Article 13 & 32/226)
important_entities.key_fact: The power of the judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts.
important_entities.significance: Though the phrase 'Judicial Review' is not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution, it is embedded in Article 13. If any law is inconsistent with Fundamental Rights or the Basic Structure, the Supreme Court/High Court can declare it ultra vires (null and void).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If an exam asks 'Where is the Basic Structure defined in the Constitution of India?', the answer is **Nowhere**. The Constitution does not define it; it is purely a judicial invention continuously evolved by the Supreme Court from case to case.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: K.B. saved the B.S. (Kesavananda Bharati saved the Basic Structure)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always link Kesavananda Bharati (1973) directly to the birth of the Basic Structure Doctrine.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains or Judiciary answers regarding Federalism or Center-State relations, you MUST cite the **S.R. Bommai guidelines** to demonstrate an understanding of the legal checks on Article 356.
